It previously exited Hong Kong. The company also lists plans for a 10MW site in Charlotte, North Carolina, a capacity totaling 40MW across Sweden, and a 500MW data center campus in Morocco. title: Lebanon s gov t plans to transform warehouse into National Data Center
text: Work is underway to clear a warehouse north of Beirut to establish a National Data Center on the site, according to Lebanese news agency Akhbar al Yawm. Telecommunications Minister Charles Hajj visited the facility in Dekwaneh with Karim Salim Salam, chief executive of telecoms firm Touch, to review the progress of the ongoing work and equipment installations as part of a rehabilitation and expansion project. This project involves relocating and merging existing Karantina and Sawwar data centers into a single location to improve operational efficiency and asset management, the news agency reported. The project is part of the Ministry of Telecommunications’ policy to utilize state-owned facilities to reduce reliance on leasing and invest in the ministry's properties.

title: Lebanon s gov t plans to transform warehouse into National Data Center
text: Hajj urged Touch to continue improving the use of available space within the facility and expedite the digitization of old documents and archives as part of the country’s digital transformation. Unused equipment and materials are being cleared from the site. Last week, the American University of Beirut (AUB) said it presented the results of a national data center benchmarking exercise to the Ministry of State for Information Technology and Artificial Intelligence (MITAI). The initiative was part of the implementation of the recently signed memorandum of understanding between AUB and MITAI to improve public sector services and accelerate Lebanon’s digital transformation.

title: Lebanon s gov t plans to transform warehouse into National Data Center
text: The benchmarking exercise was designed to address critical issues for the national digital planning, including what type of data center model is most suitable for Lebanon and the projected costs of implementing it. The findings will inform national decisions on data center strategy, capacity planning, investment priorities, and procurement models aligned with international standards. Dr. Fadi El-Jardali, managing director and co-lead of AUB’s Government Engagement Platform, said: “Despite the challenges, the team remained committed to delivering this output. This reflects a shared conviction that while crises may persist, they should not delay our preparedness for what comes next.

title: Lebanon s gov t plans to transform warehouse into National Data Center
text:
“The work presented today contributes to laying the foundations needed to position Lebanon on the digital and AI landscape.”
Lebanon does not have a notable data center market at present. According to DataCenterMap, just two facilities are in the country, both operated by LFAIT. Levanon is embroiled in the ongoing Iran war, though it is currently under a 10-day ceasefire with Israel. Despite this, reports of explosions and attacks in the country remain. National Data Centers serve as centralized locations for public sector and government workloads. At the start of this year, ground was broken on a massive data center project for the Saudi Arabian government in Riyadh. Set to span 30 million sq ft (2.78m sqm), the data center will be located in Riyadh.

text: In recent months, countries across West Africa have also notably begun investing in such initiatives, including Benin, Bamako, Mali, and two "mini data centers" in Burkina Faso. Chad has also revealed plans to invest ($204.7m) in developing a national data center and in expanding its fiber optic networks. title: Data centers as dynamic grid assets New Jersey site using solar and storage for flexibilit
text: If 90’s one-hit-wonder The New Radicals taught us anything, it’s that we only get what we give. When it comes to data centers, though, most of the conversation revolves around taking. There never seems to be enough resources, capital, or capacity. But studies have shown significant potential for integrating new load if flexibility measures are taken, and speed-to-power is a critical component of every developer’s calculus. So what if large-load customers could leverage renewable energy technology to become flexible assets and better accommodate grid conditions? Could data centers become “power plants,” in a sense? That’s exactly what Calibrant Energy is going for in its deal with Iron Mountain Data Centers.

title: Data centers as dynamic grid assets New Jersey site using solar and storage for flexibilit
text: Earlier this year, the energy solutions company signed a definitive agreement to build, own, and operate a 23 megawatt-hour (MWh) on-site battery energy storage system (BESS) at Iron Mountain’s New Jersey data center. When paired with the facility’s state-of-the-art solar array and some slick software, the 30-megawatt (MW) capacity campus becomes a unique tool and a potential blueprint for future applications. The Future of Data Centers? Located in Edison, NJ, NJE-1 is one of the largest and most resilient data centers in the Northeast, according to Iron Mountain.

title: Data centers as dynamic grid assets New Jersey site using solar and storage for flexibilit
text:
Located 30 miles from New York City, NY, and 66 miles from Philadelphia, PA, the 830,000-square-foot facility on a secure 43-acre campus provides “unmatched reliability, security, and connectivity for businesses in the Greater New York region and beyond.”
Built on a foundation of massive scale and high-performance specs, NJE-1 offers modular data center solutions for rapid deployment and flexible scaling, with multiple infrastructure configurations and systems that can be concurrently maintained. The center is billed as a connectivity hub, featuring a carrier-neutral ecosystem with 22+ carriers, major cloud on-ramps, and direct access to DE-CIX and IX-Reach. The campus is powered by Public Service Electric and Gas Company (PSE&G), New Jersey’s largest electric and natural gas utility.

title: Data centers as dynamic grid assets New Jersey site using solar and storage for flexibilit
text: The 23 MWh BESS project with Calibrant Energy adds a new layer of grid-scale flexibility. The project integrates large-scale storage with the facility’s existing 7.2 MW rooftop solar installation, an 18,000+-panel behemoth that currently holds the title of the largest photovoltaic (PV) installation at any North American data center. The result is a resilient energy ecosystem that supports Iron Mountain’s 24/7 carbon-free energy commitment with 100% renewable energy matching. “This is what the future of powering large loads looks like,” ventured Phil Martin, CEO of Calibrant Energy.

title: Data centers as dynamic grid assets New Jersey site using solar and storage for flexibilit
text:
“Customers can grow and control costs while strengthening the grid, proving that large power users are part of the energy solution rather than a burden.”
Chris Pennington, senior director of energy and sustainability at Iron Mountain, identified battery storage as a critical component in his company’s broader strategy to support the local energy ecosystem. “Flexible, on-site assets like this improve the economic and operational efficiency of the local utility grid, in addition to supporting increased reliability for all electric consumers,” he noted.

title: Data centers as dynamic grid assets New Jersey site using solar and storage for flexibilit
text:
“This project demonstrates how the data center industry can bring solutions to emerging grid challenges.”
A Dynamic Grid Asset
By using advanced real-time controls, the NJE-1 facility transforms its energy load into a dynamic asset that stabilizes the regional PSE&G grid during peak demand. This novel concept maintains uptime for Iron Mountain’s customers while eliminating the need for new, carbon-intensive power infrastructure in the local community, enabling data center clients to get online faster with reduced climate impact. As electricity demand grows, especially from digital infrastructure, there is a need for a smarter model to power large loads such as data centers, Calibrant Energy’s chief commercial officer, Matt Barnes, told Factor This.

title: Data centers as dynamic grid assets New Jersey site using solar and storage for flexibilit
text:
“This project demonstrates how distributed energy storage and advanced controls can help data centers scale responsibly while strengthening grid reliability and reducing costs in the process,” he explained. “When you unlock capacity on existing infrastructure, instead of just building costly new carbon-intensive generation resources and transmission infrastructure, that’s good for customers and for communities,” Barnes continued. “Looking ahead, the opportunity is significant, but it requires collaboration among developers, utilities, and regulators to prioritize more efficient utilization of existing grid assets alongside building new infrastructure to ensure we have the available power and resources to meet growing demand.”
Originally published in Factor This.

title: 4bn data center rejected by Nobles County Minnesota
text: A $4 billion data center has been rejected by local officials in Nobles County, Minnesota. Renewable energy developer Geronimo Power has been eyeing a 959-acre land parcel located between 200th Street and 190th Street for the construction of eight data center buildings totalling 2.5 million sq ft (232,257 sqm). But the Nobles County Commissioners’ decision to vote against a text amendment to the county’s Planning and Zoning Ordinance that would include data centers as a conditional use under the agricultural preservation designation means that Geronimo will have to look elsewhere for its project.

title: 4bn data center rejected by Nobles County Minnesota
text: According to a draft scoping document that outlines three uses for the land parcel – to leave it as is, a data center, or a mixed business development – the company’s data center would have potentially consumed between 400MW and 1GW of power. The site would have ultimately been sold to an end user who would operate the facility. Geronimo Power, formerly known as Geronimo Energy prior to May 2025, was founded in 2004 and was acquired by National Grid Ventures in 2019. The company has an operating capacity of more than 2GW, and has an additional 1GW under construction, as well as a development pipeline of more than 20GW. Nobles County is located in southern Minnesota, on the state’s border with Iowa. Comments

title: Ramping Up for POWERGEN 2027 and the 44th Annual Electric Utility Cogeneration Chemistry W
text: Already nearly one-third of 2026 has passed. Many challenges (and opportunities) continue to face the power industry; issues that will provide the foundation for POWERGEN 2027 in Salt Lake City, Utah. The call for papers for both POWERGEN and the now co-located Electric Utility & Cogeneration Chemistry (EUC2W) have been issued. To all readers, whether you might be thinking about sharing your knowledge or just wish to attend and soak up information, it is not too early to begin planning for next year. In this article, we will look at some major power generation developments, with an initial focus on several items that will be important to EUCCW attendees. Where Will the Electrons Come From?

title: Ramping Up for POWERGEN 2027 and the 44th Annual Electric Utility Cogeneration Chemistry W
text: Regarding short-term power needs, the elephant in the room is the growing electrical demand for data centers, which are proliferating throughout the country. Numerous reports suggest that gas-fired units will supply much of this power, in part related to current political headwinds towards renewables development. With time of the essence, simple cycle plants may be a common choice. From an efficiency standpoint, combined cycle power plants are preferrable, and indeed a number of newly announced projects will be of the combined cycle variety.1 Complicating factors are supply and demand issues and moving equipment fabrication through the pipeline.2 Another key component facing backlog issues are transformers.

title: Ramping Up for POWERGEN 2027 and the 44th Annual Electric Utility Cogeneration Chemistry W
text: Supporting efficiency efforts is continued development of cogeneration and combined heat & power (CHP) plants that extract much more energy from steam than conventional fossil-fired units.3 Critical at these facilities are proper makeup water treatment and steam generation chemistry control; topics that this author has addressed in previous Power Engineering articles, and which can be found on the PE website. Intriguing will be to what extent hydrogen becomes a partial or sole fuel for combustion turbines. Many arguments for and against hydrogen production viability have appeared in recent years, and the topic will definitely be on the list for POWERGEN 2027. Per reports in this publication and others, the U.S. may be moving towards a nuclear renaissance.

title: Ramping Up for POWERGEN 2027 and the 44th Annual Electric Utility Cogeneration Chemistry W
text: Small modular reactors (SMRs) appear to be a leading technology, and many people have pointed out that the U.S. Navy has successfully used small reactors for decades. SMRs and other reactor types will likely take longer to permit and build than the gas turbine technologies listed above, but they could become a solid core of future energy production. Like combined cycle and cogeneration units, diligent chemistry control, including cooling water treatment, will be extremely important. Another energy source that is heating up (pardon the pun) is geothermal. Using the earth’s natural heat is logical, but installing the underground infrastructure is not necessarily a simple task. Researchers remain undaunted, and geothermal energy production should continue to grow.

title: Ramping Up for POWERGEN 2027 and the 44th Annual Electric Utility Cogeneration Chemistry W
text:
Per an EUC2W perspective, issues related to steam purity and optimizing heat transfer will be very important. Perhaps some geothermal locations will be good spots for cogeneration facilities. Other Water Treatment and Back End Issues
Issues related to power/industrial plant water makeup, conservation and discharge treatment remain highly important. Let’s briefly examine some of these. By mandate or sometimes by choice, an increasing number of power and industrial plants are selecting municipal wastewater treatment (referred hereafter as POTW) effluent as the makeup supply to help conserve fresh water sources.

title: Ramping Up for POWERGEN 2027 and the 44th Annual Electric Utility Cogeneration Chemistry W
text: For the many POTW plants that have only primary and secondary treatment, the effluent contains organics, phosphate, ammonia, nitrite/nitrate, and other compounds in significantly higher concentrations than are normal in surface water supplies. Among the problems that these impurities can cause is their influence on microbial growth and fouling in industrial plant water systems and heat exchangers, including cooling towers. Managing microbial fouling is a challenging task even without the influence of the food and nutrients in POTW effluent. Accordingly, for industrial plants using these raw makeup supplies, some form of tertiary treatment is needed to make the water acceptable for raw makeup.

title: Ramping Up for POWERGEN 2027 and the 44th Annual Electric Utility Cogeneration Chemistry W
text: Two technologies, among others, that have emerged in recent years to remove organics and nutrients are membrane bioreactors (MBR) and moving bed bioreactors (MBBR). For this author, who has direct experience with a large industrial activated sludge treatment system and who has also observed trickling filters, MBR and MBBR are advanced versions of those technologies. But one does not just flip a switch and walk away. Proper attention is necessary to ensure reliable operation. Water conservation and recovery of plant wastewater discharge have been on the increase for years. The ultimate scenario is zero liquid discharge (ZLD), which reclaims essentially all non-biological waste water for reuse.

title: Ramping Up for POWERGEN 2027 and the 44th Annual Electric Utility Cogeneration Chemistry W
text: Space limitations prevent a detailed discussion of ZLD methods, but a key component of many systems is reverse osmosis (RO). In roughly the final three decades of the last century, RO became quite popular in the power industry as a retrofit ahead of existing makeup treatment ion exchange (IX) demineralizers to improve IX performance and reduce regeneration frequency. RO is now a standard component of makeup water treatment systems for many combined cycle power plants. In these applications, RO units typically convert 75% of the influent to purified water (permeate), with the remaining 25% as a reject stream. For waste stream recovery and ZLD applications, high recovery RO (with a 90:10 permeate-to-reject ratio or perhaps even greater) serves as a core concentrating mechanism.

title: Ramping Up for POWERGEN 2027 and the 44th Annual Electric Utility Cogeneration Chemistry W
text: The high recovery greatly reduces the volume of the remaining stream, which in turn reduces equipment and operating costs for final processes such as evaporation/crystallization. An important note, as this author knows from direct experience, stringent RO pre- and process treatment are necessary to minimize membrane fouling and scaling. Another much-discussed discharge control issue, albeit on the flue gas side, is carbon capture and sequestration (CCS). Of course, CCS is touted as a method for continued fossil fuel use with minimized CO2 emissions, but issues remain formidable. Similar to flue gas desulfurization for coal plants, a carbon capture system can be thought of as a chemical plant attached to the backend of the fossil-fired power plant.

title: Ramping Up for POWERGEN 2027 and the 44th Annual Electric Utility Cogeneration Chemistry W
text: Parasitic power usage to scrub, regenerate and compress CO2 is of concern and is a continued driver for improved capture methods. Sequestering the concentrated compound is another issue. Some facilities sit over underground formations that can hold CO2, at least according to geological analyses, but many projects call for CO2 pipelines to move the chemical elsewhere. These pipelines are controversial, and in some instances have been successfully opposed by citizens residing along the proposed pathways. CCS will be a regular discussion point for future POWERGEN conferences.

title: Ramping Up for POWERGEN 2027 and the 44th Annual Electric Utility Cogeneration Chemistry W
text:
Some Additional POWERGEN Topics
The discussion above outlined several important topics that could be a part of next year’s EUCCW (and some in main POWERGEN sessions), and the author and his colleagues would be more than glad to talk about these issues and others during the numerous networking opportunities that are part of the EUCCW. However, many other power generation topics are on the POWERGEN technical agenda and at special sessions on the exhibit floor. A comprehensive outline may be found on the POWERGEN website. Let’s consider several items. First, renewables development is not at a complete standstill, and an eventual change in presidential administration could re-energize this industry. Certainly, wind and solar generation will remain key issues at POWERGEN.

title: Ramping Up for POWERGEN 2027 and the 44th Annual Electric Utility Cogeneration Chemistry W
text: A key component of renewables growth is improvement in energy storage methods. A long-time friend of mine, and a transmission and distribution expert, never tires in pointing out that a typical coal plant maintains a 30-day fuel inventory, which is way beyond current battery capacity. More work is definitely needed to enhance renewables storage capacity. On another note, this author will be interested in seeing how biofuels (and biochemicals) technology continues to develop, apart from well-known, corn-based ethanol production. Plants/trees offer an extensive renewable resource, but issues related to land management, materials collection, transportation, and economical conversion of carbohydrates to hydrocarbons remain major R&D issues.

title: Ramping Up for POWERGEN 2027 and the 44th Annual Electric Utility Cogeneration Chemistry W
text:
For all of the generation technologies mentioned above, and others, numerous non-engineering factors will influence project development. These include:
- Supply chains and equipment procurement. Lead times have significantly lengthened. - Financing
- Permitting, siting and community engagement
- Workforce hiring
- Safety program(s) development
- Load growth planning
And, of course, another elephant in the room is the state of the electrical grid and the improvements that will be needed to bring the grid up to the standards needed for rapidly expanding electrical demand. While these are topics on the POWERGEN agenda, another primary conference is DTECH. Look for more information on the DTECH website.

title: Ramping Up for POWERGEN 2027 and the 44th Annual Electric Utility Cogeneration Chemistry W
text:
Conclusion
Many critical power generation topics will be on the agenda for POWERGEN 2027 and the accompanying EUCCW. The power industry is facing many challenges, which makes knowledge acquisition extremely important. Having worked directly in the energy sector for nearly two decades and supporting power projects for many additional years at engineering firms, I can say with confidence that POWERGEN 2027 will provide a wealth of informative details on critical power topics. title: W rtsil inks two natural gas supply deals with data center operators in Ohio and Texas
text: Finnish engine manufacturer Wärtsilä has signed two data center supply deals in Texas and Ohio. In its first deal, the company signed an agreement to supply 412MW of natural gas-powered engines to an undisclosed hyperscale data center project in Ohio. The deal will see Wärtsilä supply 40 of its 34SG (spark gas) engines, representing the company's first deal within the data center space. The delivery of the engines is expected to be completed in 2028. According to the company, the engine is ideally suited for the data center sector due to its modular nature and low water consumption, allowing for fast and easy deployment. “This project underscores the confidence data center developers place in Wärtsilä’s engine technology to deliver fast, flexible power at scale.

title: W rtsil inks two natural gas supply deals with data center operators in Ohio and Texas
text: As AI and cloud demand accelerate, operators need energy solutions that are efficient, resilient, and available on their timeline - not the grid’s. Wärtsilä provides that foundation, delivering dependable, high-performance power that scales as quickly as its infrastructure. The customer chose Wärtsilä for its proven reliability, rapid deployment, and strong operational efficiency across diverse operating conditions,” said Risto Paldanius, VP, Americas at Wärtsilä Energy. In its second deal, the company signed a 790MW supply agreement to power a data center facility under construction in Texas, USA. Wärtsilä will supply the data center operator with 42 50SG engines running on natural gas. The order was booked as intake by Wärtsilä in Q2 2026.

title: W rtsil inks two natural gas supply deals with data center operators in Ohio and Texas
text: “Wärtsilä’s primary power solutions offer significant benefits to data center developers by providing continuous, reliable primary power while using significantly less water and fuel than traditional alternatives. Also, our power solutions ramp up quickly and offer a dependable and sustainable foundation for delivering power availability, which is vital for AI and cloud operators. Our modular engine power plants allow easy capacity scale-ups, making them an ideal choice for the fast-growing data center market,” said Anders Lindberg, president of Wärtsilä Energy and EVP of Wärtsilä. The Wärtsilä equipment is scheduled for delivery in 2028, and the plant is expected to become fully operational in late 2029. This is Wärtsilä’s fifth data center-related order in the US and its first in Texas.

title: Cummins shows off new drivetrain engine tech at FDIC
text: Cummins is displaying the latest drivetrain and engine technologies for fire and rescue professionals at the Fire Department Instructors Conference (FDIC). Clarion’s own FDIC International is an annual event for fire and emergency service professionals, featuring hands-on training, educational sessions and the latest technologies. At the event, Cummins is featuring the QuikDisc Rotor, the Cummins X10 diesel engine, and its EPA27 Twin Module Aftertreatment system. “Fire and emergency vehicles must perform without hesitation,” said Obed Ruiz, General Manager of the Vocational Business at Cummins.

title: Cummins shows off new drivetrain engine tech at FDIC
text:
“Our engines and drivetrain components are built to handle the extreme demands of emergency response and help ensure first responders can rely on their equipment when every second counts.”
With QuikDisc, Cummins now supports the use of air disc brakes for single rear drive axles at the 33,500 lb capacity rating used by heavy fire apparatus, featuring a two-piece hub design. While traditional rotor replacement on heavy axles requires removing the entire wheel-end, QuikDisc requires only the rotor and its mounting flange to be removed, which can help reduce service time and labor requirements, Cummins argues.
